  • development.

questions.question: Define the mobile phase in GC and give examples.
questions.solution_html:
• In gas chromatography (GC), the mobile phase is an inert gas, called the carrier gas that
  • transports the sample through the column. Common examples include helium, nitrogen, and
  • hydrogen. The carrier gas moves the analytes through the stationary phase, where they are
  • separated based on their different physical and chemical properties
questions.final_answer: separated based on their different physical and chemical properties
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What are the benefits and limitations of starch gel electrophoresis?
questions.solution_html:
• Starch gel electrophoresis is a technique used for separating biomolecules, particularly proteins
  • and nucleic acids, based on their size and charge. Benefits: High Resolution: Provides excellent
  • separation of closely related proteins or nucleic acids.
  • Limitations: Limited Size Range, Longer Run Times, Difficult Staining
questions.final_answer: Limitations: Limited Size Range, Longer Run Times, Difficult Staining
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Define electrophoresis. Who pioneered the technique of / electrophoresis?
questions.solution_html:
• Electrophoresis is a laboratory technique that uses an electric field to move charged molecules in
  • a fluid or gel, separating them based on their size, charge, or binding affinity. It is used to
  • separate and analyze molecules like DNA, RNA, and proteins. The Swedish biochemist Arne
  • Tiselius pioneered the technique of electrophoresis in the 1930s
questions.final_answer: Tiselius pioneered the technique of electrophoresis in the 1930s
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: What is the role of centrifugation in dairy industry?

• Centrifugation plays a crucial role in the dairy industry by separating components based on

  • Separation of Cream and Milk, Clarification of Milk, Standardization of Milk
questions.final_answer: Separation of Cream and Milk, Clarification of Milk, Standardization of Milk

questions.question: What is nuclear magnetic resonance?
questions.solution_html:
• Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) is a physical phenomenon in which nuclei in a strong
  • constant magnetic field are disturbed by a weak oscillating magnetic field and respond by
  • producing an electromagnetic signal with a frequency characteristic of the magnetic field at the
  • nucleus
questions.final_answer: nucleus

questions.question: List out the factors affecting fluorescence.
questions.solution_html:
• List out the factors affecting fluorescence.
  • Factors affecting fluorescence include the intrinsic molecular structure (such as conjugation and
  • rigidity) and the external environment (like temperature, viscosity, pH, and the presence of
  • quenchers and oxygen). Other factors include concentration, the excitation wavelength, and the
  • intensity of the incident light
questions.final_answer: intensity of the incident light

questions.question: Describe the phenomenon of interaction radiation with matter.
questions.solution_html:
• The interaction of radiation with matter is the process where radiation transfers energy to or
  • changes direction in a material. This can result in absorption, where the radiation's energy is
  • completely deposited in the matter; scattering, where the radiation changes direction, often losing
  • some energy; or transmission, where the radiation passes through the material without
  • interacting. Electromagnetic radiation (e.g., X-rays, gamma rays)
questions.final_answer: interacting. Electromagnetic radiation (e.g., X-rays, gamma rays)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Give an overview of different detectors employed in HPLC
questions.solution_html:
• HPLC detectors are categorized as either selective (for specific solute properties) or universal
  • (for bulk properties), with common examples including UV/Vis, fluorescence, mass
  • spectrometry, refractive index, and electrochemical detectors
  • (5x4=(20 marks))
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain the principle, working, and applications of paper / chromatography.
questions.solution_html:
• Paper chromatography separates a mixture based on its components' different solubilities and
  • affinities for the stationary and mobile phases. The process involves a stationary phase of water
  • trapped in the paper and a mobile phase of a solvent that moves up the paper by capillary
  • action. Components of a mixture spotted on the paper are carried up by the solvent at different
  • rates, leading to their separation into distinct spots at different heights. Applications include
  • separating inks, analyzing dyes in food, testing for drug doping, and identifying pigments in
  • plants
questions.final_answer: plants
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain techniques and working of atomic absorption spectroscopy.
questions.solution_html:
• Atomic absorption spectroscopy (AAS) is an analytical technique used to measure the
  • concentration of a specific metal in a sample by atomizing it and then passing a beam of light
  • through the resulting atomic vapor.
questions.final_answer: through the resulting atomic vapor
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Write briefly about differential, rate zonal, and isopycnic centrifugation / methods.
questions.solution_html:
• Differential centrifugation: This technique separates particles primarily by size and density using
  • a series of increasing centrifugal forces. It is a simple and common method for initial purification
  • and isolating subcellular components.
  • Rate-zonal centrifugation separates particles by their sedimentation rate (size and shape), while
  • isopycnic centrifugation separates them by their buoyant density, independent of size. Rate-zonal
  • uses a shallow gradient and shorter run times, best for separating particles that differ in size but
  • not density, like organelles. Isopycnic uses a steep gradient and longer run times, ideal for
  • separating particles based on density.
questions.final_answer: separating particles based on density
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe the different modes of centrifugation.
questions.solution_html:
• The main modes of centrifugation are differential centrifugation and density gradient
  • centrifugation, with the latter often broken down into rate zonal and isopycnic
  • techniques. Differential centrifugation separates components by spinning samples at increasing
  • speeds, while density gradient centrifugation separates based on density using a prepared
  • gradient medium, which can either be separated by speed (rate zonal) or by the density at which
  • components reach equilibrium (isopycnic)
questions.final_answer: components reach equilibrium (isopycnic)
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
